teaches: When a bishop takes your knight, the recapture is a choice about what you want the position to look like for the next thirty moves, not a reflex. Taking with the g-pawn accepts doubled pawns and looks ugly; in return it opens a file, keeps both bishops aimed at open diagonals, and leaves the e-pawn free — and doubled pawns that are not weak are simply pawns.
explains: The bishop has taken on f6, which is the whole point of putting it on g5. Both recaptures are legal. Taking with the e-pawn keeps the pawns tidy but leaves the queen's bishop staring at its own pawn. Taking with the g-pawn doubles them on f7 and f6, opens the g-file, and leaves Black with the pair of bishops, since White has just given the dark-squared one away.

line: d4 Nf6 Bg5 d5 Bxf6 gxf6 e3
teaches: A pawn structure tells you which break to look for before any calculation begins. With a solid centre pawn and no dark-squared bishop opposing you, the lever against the queenside is the one that opens lines for the pieces you kept — read the structure, then find the move it asks for.
explains: White has closed the position in with the modest e-pawn, and Black's doubled f-pawns are not going anywhere. That makes the c-pawn advance the move the position wants: it strikes at the base of White's centre while the two bishops still have open diagonals to work along.
structural: reads the structure to find the break; one move, so no fork

teaches: An early rook's-pawn thrust is unsettling rather than refuting. Meet it by asking what it actually does — usually it defends the bishop's retreat square or prepares to open a file — instead of treating strangeness as danger. Being surprised is not the same as being worse.
explains: Black has hit the bishop with the knight and White, instead of retreating it, has pushed the h-pawn. Nothing is hanging and nothing is forced; the position is double-edged and both sides still have everything to play for. Advancing the d-pawn to stake out the centre is the natural, unhurried reply.
